questions.prompt: In a simplified lesion model, motor output to many arm and forearm extensors is disrupted. Which listed branch most closely matches that distribution?
explanations: Radial supplies many upper-limb extensors.
Phrenic targets the diaphragm.
Obturator serves medial-thigh muscles.
Pudendal serves perineal structures.
questions.hint: Find the upper-limb nerve associated with extension.

questions.prompt: Which plexus-to-region pairing matches the course overview?
explanations: Brachial supplies the upper limb and pectoral girdle.
The diaphragm is supplied by phrenic fibers associated with the cervical plexus.
Sacral branches supply important pelvic and lower-limb structures.
Intrinsic foot supply comes through lower-limb nerve pathways.
questions.hint: Use the regional names to orient the map.

questions.prompt: Why can injury to one named peripheral nerve affect fibers that originated at several spinal levels?
questions.model: At a plexus, fibers from multiple anterior rami mix and redistribute into peripheral nerves. A named nerve can therefore carry axons from several spinal levels, even though it supplies a recognizable peripheral territory.
questions.hint: Think about what a plexus redistributes.

questions.prompt: Which two major brachial-plexus nerves contribute motor supply to forearm or finger flexors, rather than supplying all of these flexors through one nerve?
explanations: Median and ulnar nerves supply different parts of the flexor and hand-muscle distribution.
Phrenic supplies the diaphragm; radial predominantly serves upper-limb extensor groups.
These are lower-limb nerves.
These supply gluteal-region muscles.
questions.hint: Trace the structures and distinguish the function of each part.

questions.prompt: Which pairing correctly distinguishes the gluteal nerves?
options: Superior gluteal — gluteus maximus; inferior gluteal — gluteus medius
Superior gluteal — gluteus medius/minimus; inferior gluteal — gluteus maximus
explanations: This reverses the principal pairings.
Superior gluteal supplies medius and minimus (also tensor fasciae latae); inferior gluteal supplies maximus.
Diaphragm supply is phrenic.
Forearm extensors are associated with the radial nerve.
questions.hint: Trace the structures and distinguish the function of each part.

questions.prompt: The lecture highlights semitendinosus and semimembranosus as hamstring targets. Which major nerve supplies these muscles?
explanations: Median is an upper-limb nerve.
Phrenic supplies the diaphragm.
These hamstrings receive motor supply through the sciatic nerve's tibial division.
Obturator primarily supplies medial-thigh adductors.
questions.hint: Trace the structures and distinguish the function of each part.

topics.title: Neuronal pools and circuit patterns
topics.summary: Read a neural wiring diagram by following where information branches, joins, and loops.
details: A neuronal pool is a functional group of interconnected neurons. Pools can include excitatory and inhibitory cells and can be localized or distributed.
Divergence distributes one input to multiple destinations. Convergence brings inputs from several sources to a common postsynaptic target.
Serial processing passes information through successive stages. Parallel processing works on related information along simultaneous pathways.
Reverberating circuits send collateral feedback to earlier elements, allowing activity to continue until inhibition or fatigue interrupts the cycle.
The handout labels five patterns despite a sentence saying 'Four Patterns'. Use the five illustrated categories: divergence, convergence, serial, parallel, and reverberating.

cards.front: Divergence versus convergence?
cards.back: Divergence is one input spreading to many targets; convergence is many inputs arriving at a common target.

cards.front: How does parallel processing differ from serial processing?
cards.back: Parallel pathways operate simultaneously; serial processing relays information through successive stages.

cards.front: What sustains reverberation?
cards.back: Feedback collaterals reactivate earlier circuit elements until inhibition or fatigue ends the loop.

questions.prompt: A sensory axon branches to activate several different neuronal pools. Which pattern is shown?
explanations: Convergence combines multiple inputs onto a shared target.
Divergence spreads one input to several destinations.
Reverberation requires feedback toward earlier circuit elements.
One serial chain lacks the described branching distribution.
questions.hint: Count the input and output branches.

questions.prompt: Several independent presynaptic neurons synapse on one postsynaptic neuron. What is the circuit pattern?
explanations: Divergence sends an input to several targets.
Convergence combines several sources on a shared target.
Saltatory conduction describes impulse propagation along myelinated axons.
A plexus redistributes peripheral nerve fibers rather than naming this synaptic pattern.
questions.hint: Many sources meet at one target.

questions.prompt: Which descriptions match the named circuit patterns?
options: Convergent — one source branches to many targets
explanations: Serial processing uses successive stages.
Parallel processing permits concurrent responses.
Feedback loops can prolong circuit activity.
One-to-many branching is divergence, not convergence.
questions.hint: Distinguish branching from feedback.

questions.prompt: Activity continues briefly after the initiating stimulus ends because collaterals repeatedly excite earlier neurons. Which pattern explains this?
explanations: Reverberation sustains activity through feedback.
Convergence combines sources but does not itself specify a feedback loop.
Loss of all synapses would not sustain this circuit.
Continuous conduction describes axonal propagation, not feedback between neurons.
questions.hint: Look for a circuit loop.

questions.prompt: Explain how divergence and parallel processing can help coordinate several responses to one stimulus.
questions.model: Divergence distributes the incoming information to multiple neuronal pools. Those pools can then process it in parallel, producing coordinated sensory and motor responses at similar times. The branching arrangement and simultaneous processing describe related but distinct features.
questions.hint: Separate distribution from timing.

topics.title: Reflex arcs and classification
topics.summary: Trace the five functional steps and describe a reflex using more than one classification.
details: A reflex is a rapid automatic response to a stimulus. Its arc includes receptor activation, sensory input, CNS processing, motor output, and an effector response.
Spinal sensory input enters through posterior roots; motor output exits through anterior roots. Axon collaterals can also relay information to the brain.
A monosynaptic arc has one sensory-to-motor synapse in its central pathway. Polysynaptic arcs include one or more interneurons.

Classifications describe different dimensions: innate/acquired concerns development, somatic/visceral concerns the effector, spinal/cranial concerns integration site, and mono-/polysynaptic concerns circuit complexity.
Innate does not mean completely unmodifiable. The textbook notes that higher centers and experience can modify or suppress many reflexes, qualifying the handout's absolute wording.
Reflex testing evaluates the integrity of components of a neural pathway; one altered response is not by itself a complete diagnosis.

cards.front: What are the five steps in a reflex arc?
cards.back: Receptor activation → sensory neuron → CNS processing → motor neuron → effector response.

cards.front: What does monosynaptic count?
cards.back: The single central synapse between sensory and motor neurons in the simplest arc.

cards.front: Can a reflex be both innate and somatic?
cards.back: Yes. Innate describes development; somatic describes output to skeletal muscle. The categories are independent.

questions.prompt: Arrange the five functional stages of a spinal reflex arc.
explanations: A receptor initiates sensory input, followed by central processing, motor output, and response.
questions.hint: Start with detection and end with action.

questions.prompt: A reflex uses one central synapse directly from the sensory neuron to the motor neuron. Which term describes its complexity?
explanations: Polysynaptic pathways contain multiple central synapses.
Monosynaptic means one central sensory-to-motor synapse.
Autonomic describes effector type.
Acquired describes development through learning.
questions.hint: Match the classification to synapse count.

questions.prompt: A skeletal-muscle reflex is inborn and processed in the spinal cord. Which classifications can all apply?
explanations: Inborn describes innate development.
Skeletal muscle is the somatic effector.
The stated processing site is spinal.
Visceral output acts on smooth/cardiac muscle and glands, not this skeletal-muscle target.
questions.hint: Each adjective answers a different question.

questions.prompt: Which claim best reconciles the reflex handout with the textbook's discussion of higher-center control?
options: Innate reflexes can never be influenced.
Spinal reflexes require a conscious command every time.
Many innate reflexes can be modified or suppressed by higher centers.
explanations: The textbook explicitly discusses modification and suppression.
A spinal reflex can occur without waiting for a conscious command.
Automatic spinal circuitry can still be influenced by descending inputs.
Learning does not imply a one-synapse circuit.
questions.hint: Automatic does not mean isolated from the brain.

questions.prompt: Why can a spinal reflex begin before conscious awareness while the brain still receives information about the stimulus?
questions.model: Sensory input can activate local spinal circuitry that drives motor output without waiting for conscious processing. Sensory axon collaterals and ascending pathways can simultaneously relay information to the brain, and descending pathways can modulate the reflex.
questions.hint: Consider local processing and parallel ascending information.

questions.prompt: A practiced goalkeeper's rapid learned response improves with training. In the lecture's innate-versus-acquired comparison, which description fits best?
options: Innate response present fully formed at birth
Proof that all innate reflexes are unmodifiable
explanations: The example illustrates a learned motor response; it need not be a simple spinal reflex.
The skill depends on learning.
Fast performance does not establish monosynaptic wiring.
Higher centers can influence innate reflexes; the absolute claim is incorrect.
questions.hint: Trace the structures and distinguish the function of each part.

questions.prompt: Why are the receptor and sensory-neuron stages listed separately in a reflex arc even when the receptor is a specialized ending of that neuron?
options: They perform distinct jobs: detecting the stimulus and carrying the signal toward the CNS
Every receptor must be a separate neuron
The sensory neuron must wait for a conscious decision
explanations: The functional stages differ even when they are parts of the same cell.
A receptor can be a specialized sensory ending.
The receptor detects input rather than issuing motor output.
A spinal reflex does not require a conscious command.
questions.hint: Trace the structures and distinguish the function of each part.

topics.title: Stretch, withdrawal, and crossed reflexes
topics.summary: Predict which muscles activate, which are inhibited, and which side responds.
details: Muscle spindles contain intrafusal fibers that monitor muscle length. Stretch increases sensory activity and can excite motor neurons to extrafusal fibers of the same muscle, opposing the stretch.
Gamma motor neurons adjust intrafusal fiber tension and preserve spindle sensitivity as muscle length changes; extrafusal fibers produce the main muscle force.
Golgi tendon organs monitor tension. In the textbook's tendon-reflex example, increased tension activates inhibitory pathways that reduce drive to the contracting muscle.
A flexor withdrawal reflex moves a limb away from a painful stimulus. Reciprocal inhibition reduces antagonist activity so the agonists can move the limb effectively.

During crossed extension accompanying withdrawal, the opposite limb can extend to support weight. Ipsilateral means same side; contralateral means opposite side. The combined response involves both sides.
Descending brain inputs can facilitate or inhibit spinal reflex pathways. Reflex behavior therefore reflects both the local circuit and its current modulation.

cards.front: What does a muscle spindle monitor, and what are its specialized fibers called?
cards.back: Muscle length and its changes; the spindle contains intrafusal fibers.

cards.front: What is reciprocal inhibition?
cards.back: Activation of an agonist is coordinated with inhibition of its antagonist.

cards.front: Why extend the opposite leg during withdrawal?
cards.back: Contralateral extensor activity supports body weight while the stimulated limb withdraws.

questions.prompt: A patellar tendon tap briefly stretches quadriceps. Which receptor starts the familiar stretch reflex?
explanations: Spindles detect the resulting muscle stretch.
The Golgi tendon organ is associated with tension monitoring and the separate tendon-reflex example.
The patellar stretch response does not require pain.
The motor terminal is an output site, not the initiating stretch receptor.
questions.hint: The tendon tap changes muscle length.

questions.prompt: Select all correct muscle-spindle relationships.
options: Intrafusal fibers are part of the spindle.
Gamma motor neurons adjust spindle sensitivity.
Extrafusal fibers provide the main contractile force.
Gamma motor neurons are the spindle's primary sensory afferents.
explanations: Intrafusal fibers are specialized spindle components.
Gamma efferents adjust the tension of intrafusal regions.
Extrafusal fibers are the main force-producing muscle fibers.
Gamma neurons are motor, not sensory.
questions.hint: Separate the sensor from the main force-producing fibers.

questions.prompt: During withdrawal of a hand, flexors are activated while antagonistic extensors are inhibited. What is this coordination called?
explanations: Reciprocal inhibition reduces antagonist opposition.
Saltatory conduction is node-to-node action-potential regeneration.
Convergence describes circuit inputs, not this specific antagonist coordination.
Wallerian degeneration is distal axonal breakdown after injury.
questions.hint: What prevents the antagonists from resisting withdrawal?

questions.prompt: The left foot encounters a painful stimulus and withdraws. What is the contralateral component of the associated crossed extensor response?
options: Loss of all right-leg motor activity
Contraction of both legs' flexors only
explanations: Left-leg withdrawal is the ipsilateral component.
Extension on the opposite side supports balance during withdrawal.
The opposite limb must generate support, not lose all activity.
Flexing both legs would not supply the described support.
questions.hint: Contralateral means opposite to the stimulus.

questions.prompt: Compare spindle-mediated stretch reflexes with the textbook's Golgi tendon reflex example.
questions.model: A muscle spindle monitors muscle length; stretch can drive contraction of the same muscle to oppose lengthening. A Golgi tendon organ monitors tension, and in the textbook's tendon-reflex example inhibitory interneurons reduce motor drive to that muscle. The receptors and central effects differ.
questions.hint: Contrast the measured variable and the motor outcome.

questions.prompt: Why can interneuron branches spread withdrawal-reflex activity to several spinal segments?
options: To coordinate several muscles in moving away from the stimulus
To turn all spinal nerves into sensory-only nerves
To require conscious approval before withdrawal
To prevent sensory information from reaching the brain
explanations: A protective movement can recruit muscles supplied from more than one segment.
Spinal nerves remain mixed.
Local spinal coordination can occur without waiting for conscious processing.
Ascending information can accompany the local response.
questions.hint: Trace the structures and distinguish the function of each part.
